stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Most speakers of American English believe they pronounce the t in “top” and the t in “water” ______ acoustic recordings show that the t in “water” is usually a rapid tap of the tongue, closer to a d than to the crisp burst of air heard in “top.” The tap is so brief, lasting only a few hundredths of a second, that many listeners never notice it.
explanation: Both sides of the blank are complete sentences. “Most speakers… believe they pronounce the t… identically” can stand alone, and so can “acoustic recordings show that…”. Two sentences need a strong break such as a semicolon, and “however” starts the second sentence because that is where the contrast with the speakers' belief begins. The semicolon goes before “however,” and a comma follows it.

A.why: You treated “however” like “but” and joined two complete sentences with commas alone. That is a comma splice. Unlike “but,” the word “however” can't link two sentences on its own.

C.why: You put no punctuation at all where the first sentence ends, so the two sentences run together. “However” needs a semicolon or period in front of it here.

D.why: You attached “however” to the wrong clause. Putting the semicolon after it makes “however” end the first sentence, which is the opening of the passage, so it has nothing earlier to contrast with. The contrast belongs to the recordings, so “however” has to start that clause.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Nineteenth-century folklorists often presented the tales they published as the authentic voice of illiterate rural storytellers. Many of the tales in Anders Halvorsen's celebrated 1852 ______ from educated townspeople who had read earlier printed versions and retold them from memory. Letters preserved in Halvorsen's archive name several of these informants, among them a schoolteacher and a pharmacist's wife.
explanation: No sentence ends at this blank. The subject “Many of the tales in… collection” hasn't reached its verb “came” yet. Here “however” only interrupts one clause, so it gets a comma on each side. If you cross it out, you're left with “Many of the tales in… collection came from educated townspeople,” which is a complete, correct sentence.

B.why: You reached for a semicolon because “however” was there. A semicolon has to sit between two complete sentences, but “Many of the tales in Anders Halvorsen's celebrated 1852 collection” is only a subject with no verb, so it's a fragment.

C.why: You moved the strong break to after “however,” but it still cuts the subject off from its verb “came.” Neither side of that semicolon is a complete sentence.

D.why: You closed the interruption without opening it. An interrupting “however” needs matching commas on both sides, and this choice has only one.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: On a Mercator projection, any straight line drawn between two ports corresponds to a single, constant compass ______ a navigator could plot an entire ocean crossing with little more than a ruler and a protractor. The price of this convenience is severe distortion of area near the poles, which makes Greenland appear nearly as large as Africa.
explanation: The first sentence ends at “bearing.” “A navigator could plot…” has its own subject and verb, so it's a second complete sentence. “Therefore” introduces the consequence, so it belongs at the start of that second sentence: semicolon before it, comma after it.

A.why: You let commas do the work of a semicolon. “Therefore” isn't a joining word like “so,” so commas around it still leave a comma splice between two complete sentences.

B.why: You left out punctuation where the first sentence ends, so the two sentences fuse into a run-on.

C.why: You attached “therefore” to the first clause. That makes the opening sentence of the passage claim to be a conclusion from something that was never said. The result is what the navigator could do, so “therefore” has to start that clause.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The Arctic tern weighs little more than a deck of ______ tracking studies have shown that individual birds fly tens of thousands of kilometers each year, shuttling between breeding grounds in the Arctic and feeding grounds off Antarctica. Over a lifespan of thirty years, a single tern may travel a distance equal to several round trips to the Moon.
explanation: “The Arctic tern weighs little more than a deck of cards” is a complete sentence, and so is “tracking studies have shown…”. “Even so” concedes the bird's small size and introduces the surprising distance, so it opens the second sentence. That means a period before it and a comma after it.

A.why: You treated “even so” like “but” and used only commas between two complete sentences, which makes a comma splice.

B.why: You put nothing where the first sentence ends, so the two sentences run together.

D.why: You put the period after “even so,” so it ends the first sentence instead of opening the second. As the passage's first sentence, it has nothing earlier to concede to. The surprise is the long flight, and that's where “even so” belongs.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Prints made by wood engraving can look much like woodcuts, since both are printed from the raised surface of a carved block. The two methods differ considerably ______ cut into the hard end grain of the wood rather than its softer side grain, a choice that allows them to carve lines as fine as a strand of hair.
explanation: In this sentence “though” is a trailing contrast word. It belongs to “The two methods differ considerably,” and it contrasts with the similarity described in the sentence before. That clause is complete, and what follows explains how the methods differ, so a colon after “though” correctly introduces the explanation.

A.why: You attached “though” to the wrong clause. The contrast is with the previous sentence about the prints looking alike, so “though” trails “differ considerably.” Moving it after the semicolon leaves “Though, engravers cut…”, which isn't standard.

C.why: You set “though” off with commas and then kept going into a second complete sentence. “Engravers cut into…” has its own subject and verb, so a bare comma there is a comma splice.

D.why: You dropped the comma before “though” and still joined two complete sentences with only a comma, which makes a comma splice.
